reasoning: Erbo explains that Ørsted's revised strategy focuses exclusively on bottom-fixed offshore wind, having exited floating wind, green fuels, and onshore Europe. He does believe floating wind will eventually be commercially viable but thinks the timeline is significantly longer than consensus expects, particularly given current affordability pressures on consumers. The LCOE of floating is materially higher than bottom-fixed, making it unattractive unless a market has no alternative. He views the company's competitive advantage as strongest in bottom-fixed, where growth is most certain.
quote: Our view is that with the points I mentioned before about it being a global supply chain, the European supply chain can deliver the build out that we see right now. Would it be possible for you as a state, partly state owned company to buy anything else than European? If you came and just say, hey, guys, we're just going to buy Chinese turbines now. Would you keep your job? Right now, when you look at the frameworks in Europe, if Chinese turbines is not part of the mix... The reason we stepped away from floating for us is not because we don't believe, I don't believe it will come. I certainly believe it will come. But I think it's going to take more time than people expect. Is there a good business case for it? There can be one day, I don't see it right now for us at least. Back to what we talked about before, it's about affordability. It's about cheap power for the consumers. And at a point in time where there is so much in focus, then the LCOE of floating is simply significantly higher than it is for bottom fixed.

So I think sort of the electrification demand for Europe is going to be massive in the decades to come... I think the premise behind that question is that there is an either or. If you agree with me that electricity demand, it doesn't even have to double. But let's just assume that it's going to go up with 1% to 2% for the next 15 years. You need it all. headline: Ørsted CEO concedes US offshore wind was a costly strategic mistake — stop work order on an 80%-complete project highlights political risk of long-cycle energy infrastructure in the US
reasoning: Erbo describes receiving a stop work order on 22 August 2025 on a US offshore wind project that was 80% complete, comparing it to building a bridge and being stopped 50 metres before the toll terminal. Ørsted subsequently filed a lawsuit against the US government on 4 September. He acknowledges in retrospect that Ørsted set the bar too high at its June 2023 capital markets day, was too focused on volume rather than value, and did not exit the US fast enough when warning signs emerged. The company had spent seven to nine years obtaining permits, making the write-downs particularly damaging. He now emphasises that projects must be structured so the company can afford to step back at any given time.
quote: Should you have been in this project in the first place? Of course, Nagel and I, when you look at it now, and when you look at the implications on Earth, not only that project, but also our ocean wind project that we stepped away from in the US and our sunrise project that we are constructing now. Of course, Earth would have been better off without. That's pretty obvious. If you were to be self-critical, what would you say the mistake was? I think that the way I look at it is where I think what we should have done is that we should have been able to, we should have stepped back soon. So if I look at those sort of the, we had a capital market stay in June 23 where we set the bar high. We took the right down on ocean wind in the US in the fall of that year. We set the bar too high on the capital market stay. We were too focused on volume rather than value. And then we didn't step away fast enough when we saw starting to see the writings on the role in the US.
